title: Likelihood is cross-entropy
objectives: Show that maximising the likelihood minimises the cross-entropy to the data, in nats or in bits.

screens.prose: A coin lands heads 7 times in 10 tosses. In estimation you found $\hat\theta = 0.7$ by maximising the likelihood. The curve shows the average loss $-\tfrac1{10}\sum \log_2 q_\theta(x_i)$ for a coin model $\theta$.
screens.question: Drag the point to the bottom of the curve.

hints.text: The bottom is where the curve turns from falling to rising.
It is near the share of heads in the data.

feedback.correct: The loss is least at $\theta = 0.7$: the maximum likelihood estimate again.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Slide along the curve until it stops falling.

byKey.fair: You stopped at the fair coin. The data has 7 heads in 10, so the curve keeps falling past 0.5.

explain.text: The lowest average loss, 0.881 bits a toss, comes at $\theta = 0.7$. The likelihood peaked at the same $\theta$, because the loss is minus its log, averaged.

screens.prose: The average loss is the **average negative log-likelihood**. With 7 heads and 3 tails it is $-(0.7 \log_2 \theta + 0.3 \log_2(1 - \theta))$: a cross-entropy, with the data's shares $\hat p = (0.7, 0.3)$ as the truth.
screens.question: What is the average loss of the fair-coin model, $\theta = 0.5$, in bits?

hints.text: Under the fair model each outcome has chance 0.5.
Weigh 1 by 0.7 and 0.3: the total is 1.

feedback.correct: Every toss costs $-\log_2 0.5 = 1$ bit, so the average is 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Under $\theta = 0.5$ both outcomes have chance one half.

byKey.entropy: That is the minimum, at $\theta = 0.7$. The fair model costs more.
byKey.total: That is the total over 10 tosses. The loss is an average.
byKey.nats: That is in nats. In bits, $-\log_2 0.5 = 1$.

screens.prose: At the bottom, $\theta = 0.7$ equals the data's own shares $\hat p = (0.7, 0.3)$. A cross-entropy with $q = \hat p$ is just an entropy.
screens.question: What is the average loss at $\theta = 0.7$, in bits? Give a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.correct: $H(0.7, 0.3) \approx 0.881$ bits: the curve touches the dashed entropy line.

byKey.theta: That is where the minimum is, not its height.

explain.text: $0.7 \times 0.515 + 0.3 \times 1.737 \approx 0.881$ bits. The minimum of the cross-entropy is the entropy of the data.

screens.prose: Code that fits models works in nats: the average loss with $\ln$ in place of $\log_2$.
screens.question: What is the minimum average loss in nats? Give a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.correct: $0.8813 \times 0.6931 \approx 0.611$ nats: the same minimum, at the same $\theta$.

byKey.divided: You divided by $\ln 2$. Nats are fewer than bits.

explain.text: $-(0.7 \ln 0.7 + 0.3 \ln 0.3) \approx 0.611$ nats. Changing the unit scales the whole curve, so the minimiser stays at 0.7.

screens.prose: Why is the average negative log-likelihood a cross-entropy? Write it for the 10 tosses: $$-\frac1{10}\sum_{i=1}^{10} \log_2 q_\theta(x_i).$$
screens.question: Which step turns it into $-(0.7 \log_2 \theta + 0.3 \log_2(1 - \theta))$?

options.text: Group the equal terms, then divide each count by 10
Use Jensen's inequality to move the log outside the sum
options.why: No inequality is used: the two sides are equal term for term.

options.text: Use the rule that the log of a product is a sum of logs
options.why: That step came earlier, from the likelihood to the log-likelihood.

options.text: Set $\theta = 0.7$ in every one of the ten terms
options.why: The identity holds for every $\theta$, not only at 0.7.

hints.text: Seven of them are the same.

feedback.correct: Counting equal terms turns $\tfrac1n\sum$ over tosses into $\sum$ over outcomes, weighted by their shares $\hat p$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Look at what the ten terms are.

byKey.jensen: You reached for an inequality. This step is an exact regrouping.

explain.text: Seven tosses contribute $\log_2 \theta$ and three $\log_2(1 - \theta)$. So the average is $-\sum_x \hat p(x) \log_2 q_\theta(x) = H(\hat p, q_\theta)$.

screens.prose: Every time, the average loss was a cross-entropy to the data: $$-\tfrac1n \sum_i \log q_\theta(x_i) = H(\hat p, q_\theta) = H(\hat p) + D(\hat p \| q_\theta).$$ $H(\hat p)$ does not move with $\theta$. So maximising the likelihood minimises the cross-entropy, and the KL divergence to the data.
screens.question: If some $\theta$ makes $q_\theta = \hat p$, what is the least average loss?

options.text: $H(\hat p)$, the entropy of the data

options.why: The loss is 0 only if every outcome was certain. Here it bottoms out at $H(\hat p)$.
That is the gap above the minimum, which is 0 at $q_\theta = \hat p$.

feedback.correct: At $q_\theta = \hat p$ the KL term is 0 and the loss is $H(\hat p)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which term of the sum can reach 0?

explain.text: $D(\hat p \| q_\theta) \ge 0$, with equality only at $q_\theta = \hat p$ (l6). So the least average loss is $H(\hat p)$, 0.881 bits for the coin.

screens.prose: A colleague fits the same coin model to a second sample of 100 tosses with 70 heads. He reports the total loss: 88.13 bits, against 8.81 bits on the first sample.
screens.question: Does the model fit the second sample worse?

options.text: No: per toss, both are 0.881 bits

options.why: Ten times as many tosses give ten times the total. Divide by the number of tosses.

options.text: No: it fits the second sample ten times better
options.why: The fit is the same, 0.881 bits a toss.

hints.text: How many tosses are in each sample?
Divide each total by its count.
Both come to 0.881 bits a toss.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide each total by its number of tosses.

byKey.yes: You compared totals over samples of different size. Compare averages.

explain.text: $88.13 / 100 = 8.813 / 10 = 0.881$ bits a toss. Summing or averaging gives the same minimiser, but only averages compare across samples.

screens.prose: Now the model is not allowed past $\theta = 0.6$. The data still has $\hat p = (0.7, 0.3)$, so the best allowed coin is on the boundary, 0.6. There the loss is $0.881 + D(\hat p \| q_{0.6})$.
screens.question: What is the gap $D(\hat p \| q_{0.6})$, in bits? Give a decimal to 3 places.

hints.text: $\hat p / q$ is $0.7/0.6$ for heads and $0.3/0.4$ for tails.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out $\sum \hat p \log_2(\hat p / q)$ with $q = (0.6, 0.4)$.

byKey.loss: That is the whole loss at 0.6. Subtract the entropy 0.881.
byKey.reversed: You weighed by the model. The data's shares are the weights.

explain.text: The loss at 0.6 is 0.912 bits, and $0.912 - 0.881 = 0.031$. A model family that cannot reach $\hat p$ pays a KL gap.

screens.prose: A quant forecasts the chance of an up day with one constant $\theta$. She scores it by log loss, the average negative log-likelihood in nats. Over 250 days the share rose on 150.
screens.question: What is the least log loss any constant forecast can reach, in nats per day? Give a decimal to 3 places.

hints.text: The best constant is the share of up days.

feedback.correct: The best constant is $\theta = 0.6$, with log loss $-(0.6 \ln 0.6 + 0.4 \ln 0.4) \approx 0.673$ nats.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The best constant is the share of up days; its loss is the entropy of the data.

byKey.fair: That is the forecast 0.5, at $\ln 2$. The share 0.6 does a little better.
byKey.bits: That is in bits. Log loss uses nats.

explain.text: Fitting $\theta$ by log loss is maximum likelihood: $\hat\theta = 150/250 = 0.6$. Its loss, 0.673 nats, is $H(\hat p)$; every loss in this strand works the same way.

ideas: The average negative log-likelihood of data under $q_\theta$ is the cross-entropy $H(\hat p, q_\theta)$, with $\hat p$ the data's shares.
It equals $H(\hat p) + D(\hat p \| q_\theta)$, so maximising the likelihood minimises the KL divergence to the data; the least is $H(\hat p)$ when $q_\theta$ can reach $\hat p$.
Bits or nats scale the loss, not its minimiser. Compare averages, not totals; a family that cannot reach $\hat p$ pays a KL gap.

formula.name: Likelihood as cross-entropy
formula.tex: -\tfrac1n \sum_i \log q_\theta(x_i) = H(\hat p) + D(\hat p \| q_\theta)

summary.trap: Comparing total losses on samples of different sizes, or mixing bits and nats between two models.
